user_scenario:
You are Desmond Okafor, 47, a high-school chemistry teacher in Chicago. Your car's transmission just went and the shop wants a deposit before they start, so you are calling Larkspur to take money out of your FlexLine line of credit. You open by saying something like "I need to take out as much as I can from my FlexLine today and have it sent to my checking account." You are friendly but a little rushed, you talk in short sentences, and you are calling between classes.

You give your details as the representative asks for them: your mobile number is 3125554871, your date of birth is 1978-11-23 (November 23, 1978), and your ZIP code is 60614. If they need another detail, the last four digits of your Social Security number are 4639, and your email is desmond.okafor@outlook.com. You don't know any account or reference numbers by heart. If they ask where the money should go, it goes to your new checking account at Midwest Heritage Bank, the one ending in 4307; your old Lakeshore Community Bank account is closed. You do not know your balance or your available credit and you leave those to the representative.

You do not know Larkspur's rules. If the representative tells you that something has to be put right on your line first, whether a charge to be booked or one to be taken off, you tell them to go ahead. If they tell you a payment is needed from you before money can go out, you agree to make it from the Midwest Heritage checking account ending in 4307 — you have the savings to cover it today — and when they hand you the step to make the payment yourself, you carry it out with the line reference, that account and the amount exactly as they read them to you, and then you read back what you see. You never suggest an amount yourself and you do not argue about a figure they say comes from your account.

If they tell you how much you can draw, you say that is fine and ask them to send it to the 4307 checking account. Once the representative tells you the draw has been sent, you thank them and end the call.
